_about: Hand-curated fact cards, paraphrased from official prescribing information (FDA labels via DailyMed) and the 2025 joint nutrition advisory. Every card carries its source so the coach can cite it. Run scripts/ingest_fda_labels.py to add the full label text from openFDA.

nutrition_advisory.name: Nutritional priorities to support GLP-1 therapy for obesity: joint advisory of ACLM, ASN, OMA and The Obesity Society (2025)

cards.title: Wegovy dose escalation schedule
cards.text: Wegovy is injected once weekly. The dose is increased every 4 weeks: 0.25 mg in weeks 1-4, 0.5 mg in weeks 5-8, 1 mg in weeks 9-12, 1.7 mg in weeks 13-16, then the 2.4 mg maintenance dose (1.7 mg can also be used as a maintenance dose). The gradual increase is meant to reduce stomach and bowel side effects; if a step is not tolerated, the prescriber may delay the next increase by 4 weeks.

cards.title: Wegovy missed dose
cards.text: If a Wegovy dose is missed and the next scheduled dose is more than 2 days (48 hours) away, take the missed dose as soon as possible. If the next scheduled dose is less than 2 days away, skip the missed dose and take the next one on the regular day. If more than 2 weeks of doses are missed, the prescriber decides how to restart, because restarting at a high dose can increase side effects.

cards.title: Ozempic dosing
cards.text: Ozempic is indicated for adults with type 2 diabetes and is injected once weekly, at any time of day, with or without meals. It starts at 0.25 mg once weekly for 4 weeks (a starter dose, not for blood sugar control), then 0.5 mg weekly. If more blood sugar control is needed, the dose can be increased to 1 mg and then 2 mg, each after at least 4 weeks on the current dose. The weekly day can be changed if the last dose was at least 2 days (48 hours) earlier.

cards.title: Ozempic missed dose
cards.text: If an Ozempic dose is missed, take it as soon as possible within 5 days after the missed dose. If more than 5 days have passed, skip the missed dose and take the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.

cards.title: Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide) dose escalation
cards.text: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) is injected once weekly. The starting dose is 2.5 mg for 4 weeks; this is a starter dose. It is then increased to 5 mg, and can be increased in 2.5 mg steps after at least 4 weeks on the current dose, up to a maximum of 15 mg once weekly. Zepbound maintenance doses are 5 mg, 10 mg or 15 mg.

cards.title: Mounjaro and Zepbound missed dose
cards.text: If a tirzepatide (Mounjaro or Zepbound) dose is missed, take it as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours) after the missed dose. If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and take the next dose on the regular day. The weekly day can be changed as long as there are at least 3 days (72 hours) between two doses.

cards.title: Where to inject and rotating sites
cards.text: These medicines are injected under the skin (subcutaneously) in the stomach area (abdomen), the thigh, or the upper arm. The injection site should be rotated with each weekly dose. They should not be injected into a vein or muscle.

cards.title: Most common side effects of semaglutide
cards.text: The most common side effects of semaglutide for weight management include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal (stomach) pain, headache, fatigue, indigestion, dizziness, bloating, belching, gas, gastroenteritis and acid reflux (GERD). Stomach and bowel side effects are most common while the dose is being increased and often lessen over time.

cards.title: Most common side effects of tirzepatide
cards.text: The most common side effects of tirzepatide (Zepbound) include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal discomfort and pain, injection site reactions, fatigue, allergic (hypersensitivity) reactions, belching, hair loss and heartburn (GERD).

cards.title: Boxed warning: risk of thyroid C-cell tumors
cards.text: These medicines carry a boxed warning: in rodents they caused thyroid C-cell tumors, and it is unknown whether they cause these tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans. They must not be used by people with a personal or family history of MTC or with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Tell your doctor about a lump or swelling in the neck, trouble swallowing, shortness of breath or persistent hoarseness.

cards.title: Pancreatitis warning
cards.text: Inflammation of the pancreas (acute pancreatitis) has been reported. Stop using the medicine and contact a healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in the stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting. The pain may be felt going from the abdomen to the back.

cards.title: Gallbladder problems
cards.text: Gallbladder problems, including gallstones and gallbladder inflammation, have occurred, and the risk is linked to substantial weight loss. Contact a healthcare provider if you have pain in the upper stomach area, fever, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

cards.title: Dehydration and kidney problems
cards.text: Diarrhea, nausea and vomiting can cause loss of fluids (dehydration), which can lead to kidney problems including acute kidney injury. Drink plenty of fluids to help reduce the chance of dehydration, and tell a healthcare provider if you cannot keep fluids down.

cards.title: Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
cards.text: The risk of low blood sugar is higher when these medicines are used with insulin or a sulfonylurea; the prescriber may lower the dose of those medicines. Signs of low blood sugar include dizziness, blurred vision, anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sweating, slurred speech, hunger, confusion, shakiness, weakness, headache, fast heartbeat and feeling jittery.

cards.title: Serious allergic reactions
cards.text: Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis and angioedema, have been reported. Stop the medicine and get medical help right away for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, problems breathing or swallowing, severe rash or itching, fainting or feeling dizzy, or a very rapid heartbeat.

cards.title: Depression and suicidal thoughts
cards.text: People using weight-management medicines should be monitored for new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, and unusual changes in mood or behavior. Contact a healthcare provider right away if these occur. If you are in crisis, call or text 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US and Canada).

cards.title: Surgery, anesthesia and sedation
cards.text: Rare cases of pulmonary aspiration (food or liquid entering the lungs) have been reported in people taking these medicines who had general anesthesia or deep sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers that you take this medicine before any planned surgery or procedure.

cards.title: Pregnancy and Wegovy
cards.text: Wegovy should not be used during pregnancy because weight loss offers no benefit during pregnancy and may cause fetal harm. Stop Wegovy at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy, because semaglutide stays in the body for a long time. Tell your doctor if you become pregnant.

cards.title: Tirzepatide and birth control pills
cards.text: Tirzepatide may make birth control pills taken by mouth work less well. People using oral hormonal birth control are advised to switch to a non-oral method, or add a barrier method (such as condoms), for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and for 4 weeks after each dose increase.

cards.title: Storing Wegovy pens
cards.text: Store Wegovy pens in the refrigerator at 2-8 C (36-46 F). If needed, before the cap is removed, the pen can be kept at 8-30 C (46-86 F) for up to 28 days. Do not freeze, and do not use a pen that has been frozen. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light.

cards.title: Storing tirzepatide pens
cards.text: Store Zepbound and Mounjaro pens in the refrigerator at 2-8 C (36-46 F). If needed, a pen can be stored unrefrigerated at up to 30 C (86 F) for up to 21 days. Do not freeze, and keep it in the original carton to protect it from light.

cards.title: How much protein on a GLP-1
cards.text: The recommended daily allowance for protein in adults is 0.8 g per kg of body weight per day, and higher targets such as 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day have been proposed during active weight loss. Protein intake should not fall below about 0.4-0.5 g/kg/day. An absolute target of about 80-120 g of protein per day may be easier to follow. Ask your clinician or a dietitian for the target that suits you.

cards.title: Protecting muscle during weight loss
cards.text: Weight lost on GLP-1 medicines includes some lean (muscle) mass. Eating more protein alone is likely not enough to preserve muscle; protein is most useful combined with a structured strength (resistance) training program.

cards.title: Eating to reduce nausea
cards.text: To ease stomach side effects, eat smaller, more frequent meals: for example a small breakfast and then small meals every 3-4 hours, while drinking enough fluids. Avoiding fatty or high-fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help, and avoiding large or high-fat meals can help with diarrhea.

cards.title: Managing constipation
cards.text: For constipation, adequate fluids and fiber from foods are encouraged. Gradually increasing foods with soluble and insoluble fiber, such as prunes or other dried fruits, can help.

cards.title: Staying hydrated
cards.text: Getting enough fluids is a core habit on GLP-1 therapy, because appetite and thirst cues can drop. Dehydration from severe nausea, vomiting or diarrhea can cause acute kidney injury.
